operative_clauses.judgment_reason: The single operative clause (the amendment of Instructions section XV-4 and Consular Regulations section 451 with the prohibition on accepting presents from foreign governments) ended on 1940-04-18, when Executive Order 8396 expressly revoked Executive Order 7577 of March 19, 1937 without condition. The date is the signing date of Executive Order 8396; that order states no separate effective date and was filed on April 19 and published on April 20, 1940. The held text shows no earlier ending: the order has no own end, and no earlier instrument that names it was found. The amending command was performed on issue, and the express revocation is the event that ended the order itself.

B y virtue o f and pursuant to thé authority vested in me  
by section 1752 of the Revised Statutes (U . S . C ., title 22,  
sec. 1 32), it is ordered th at section X V -4  o f the Instructions 
to Diplom atic Officers and section 451 of the Consular Regu­
lations be, and they are hereby, amended to read as follow s: *
“ Presents and testimonials. — No diplomatic or consular  
officer shall ask or accept for himself or any other per­
son, any present, em olument, office, or title of any kind  
from  any king, prince, or foreign state. (U . S. Const.,  
A rt. I, sec. 9, el. 8, U . S . C ., title 22, § 126.) Any present,  
decoration, order, or testim onial in acknowledgment of  
services rendered to th e citizens or governments  
of foreign states, or other thing, which shall be con - j 
ferred on or presented by any foreign government to  
any officer of the United States, shall be tendered through  
the Departm ent of State, and not to the individual in  
person, but such present, decoration, or other thing shall  
not be delivered by the Departm ent of State unless so  
authorized by act of Congress. (5 U . S. C ., § 115.)
“ Thorough consideration was given by the Committee  
on Foreign Affairs of the House o f Representatives in  
1934 to  the question whether the Congress should consent  
to the acceptance of presents, decorations, orders, medals,  
testim onials, or other things. I t resulted in  the enact­
m ent o f the join t resolution approved June 27, 1934 (48  
S ta t. 1267 ), which authorized only certain retired offi­
cers and employees therein nam ed to accept such decora­
tions, orders, m edals, or presents as had been tendered  
to them  by foreign governments. Hence it appears to be  
the settled policy of the Congress to decline to authorize  
the acceptance by civilian officers of the Government in  
active service of presents, decorations, medals, orders,  
testim onials, or other things, when presented to or con­
ferred on such officers by any king, prince, or foreign  
state. Furthermore, it  is contrary to the policy of the  
Governm ent to tender or to award presents, decorations,  
m edals, orders, testim onials, or other things to re p re -.  
sentatives of foreign governments. In  view of the atti­
tude of the Congress and the policy of the Government,  
Am erican diplom atic and consular officers are hereby  
prohibited  from  accepting in any circum stances  any  
present, decoration, m edal, order, testim onial, or other 
thing th at m ay be tendered to them by any foreign king,  
prince, or foreign state.”

research_rationale:
I read the complete held Federal Register original of Executive Order 7577 (2 FR 671, March 24, 1937; signed March 19, 1937). It is one order that amends section XV-4 of the Instructions to Diplomatic Officers and section 451 of the Consular Regulations to read as a new text on presents and testimonials, and that text prohibits diplomatic and consular officers from accepting any present, decoration, medal, order or testimonial from a foreign king, prince or state. It has no duration, condition, report or savings language. I read the complete held Federal Register text of Executive Order 8396 (5 FR 1461, April 20, 1940; signed April 18, 1940). Under its heading revoking executive orders, it states that the listed executive orders are revoked, and the list includes Executive Order No. 7577 dated March 19, 1937, with no condition, exception or deferred effective date. That express revocation is the first end of the order. I read the coverage notes of the three machine searches before selecting them: the U.S. Code search (edition through 2026-10-09, so laws enacted in the last five days before the 2026-10-14 cutoff are not reflected) and the eCFR search (as of 2026-10-14) found no citation of this order, and the Federal Register disposition-note search found the revocation by Executive Order 8396 and a catalog note that is blank about its effect, which the held revocation text supplies. No held instrument restores or revives Executive Order 7577 after the revocation. I read the complete held Federal Register original of Executive Order 8129 (4 FR 1997-1998, May 12, 1939; signed May 10, 1939): it reserves 144.30 acres in Benson County, North Dakota, for the use of the Department of Agriculture as the Minnewastena Migratory Waterfowl Refuge, makes it unlawful to hunt, trap, capture or disturb any bird or wild animal within the refuge or to enter it except under rules prescribed by the Secretary of Agriculture, and names the refuge. It has no duration, condition or sunset. I read the complete text of Public Land Order 1704 (23 FR 6110, Federal Register of August 9, 1958). Its title and operative paragraph revoke Executive Orders 8123, 8126, 8129 and 8163, which reserved lands for the Department of Agriculture as migratory waterfowl refuges, and it repeats the tract description of Executive Order 8129 (sec. 12, lot 7 and SW1/4SE1/4, and sec. 13, lot 1 and NW1/4NE1/4, T. 152 N., R. 65 W.). It is signed by the Assistant Secretary of the Interior on August 5, 1958, acting under Executive Order 10355, and has no partial limiter, exception or deferred effective date. That is the first end. The Federal Register disposition note dates the revocation August 4, 1958, but the order's own signature line reads August 5, 1958, so the held text controls. An earlier unnamed instrument, Reorganization Plan No. II of 1939 (section 4(f)), made effective July 1, 1939 by Public Resolution No. 20, transferred the Bureau of Biological Survey and wildlife functions from Agriculture to Interior. It does not name this order, so under the owner ruling on unnamed instruments it is recorded as a later event and a disclosed earlier candidate, not as the end. I read the coverage notes of the three machine searches before selecting them: the U.S. Code search (through 2026-10-09) and the eCFR search (as of 2026-10-14) found no citation of this order, and the disposition-note search found only the Public Land Order 1704 revocation. The Federal Register text layers are machine extracted and were checked only as text; the page images were not inspected.

research_rationale:
I read the complete held Federal Register original of Executive Order 8163 (4 FR 2409, June 15, 1939; signed June 12, 1939): it reserves 640.00 acres in Walsh County, North Dakota, for the use of the Department of Agriculture as the Pioneer Lake Migratory Waterfowl Refuge, makes it unlawful to hunt, trap, capture or disturb any bird or wild animal within the refuge or to enter it except under rules prescribed by the Secretary of Agriculture, and names the refuge. It has no duration, condition or sunset. I read the complete text of Public Land Order 1704 (23 FR 6110, Federal Register of August 9, 1958). Its title and operative paragraph revoke Executive Orders 8123, 8126, 8129 and 8163, which reserved lands for the Department of Agriculture as migratory waterfowl refuges, and it repeats the tract description of Executive Order 8163 (sec. 21, T. 155 N., R. 58 W.). It is signed by the Assistant Secretary of the Interior on August 5, 1958, acting under Executive Order 10355, and has no partial limiter, exception or deferred effective date. That is the first end. The Federal Register disposition note dates the revocation August 4, 1958, but the order's own signature line reads August 5, 1958, so the held text controls. An earlier unnamed instrument, Reorganization Plan No. II of 1939 (section 4(f)), made effective July 1, 1939 by Public Resolution No. 20, transferred the Bureau of Biological Survey and wildlife functions from Agriculture to Interior. It does not name this order, so under the owner ruling on unnamed instruments it is recorded as a later event and a disclosed earlier candidate, not as the end. I read the coverage notes of the three machine searches before selecting them: the U.S. Code search (through 2026-10-09) and the eCFR search (as of 2026-10-14) found no citation of this order, and the disposition-note search found only the Public Land Order 1704 revocation. The Federal Register text layers are machine extracted and were checked only as text; the page images were not inspected.
